profile.summary: Ruth presents how God's faithfulness manifests itself in common and painful situations of everyday life. In the midst of hunger, grief, displacement and vulnerability, Naomi returns to Bethlehem accompanied by his Moabite daughter-in-law, Ruth, whose loyalty stands out. In the field of Boaz, a kind relative, the divine provision begins to reveal itself through concrete acts of generosity, protection and family responsibility. The book culminates with public redemption, Ruth's marriage to Boaz and the birth of Obed, bringing security to Naomi and inserting this family in David's lineage. The work concludes by showing that simple events can have lasting reach in God's plan.
profile.setting: The events take place around 1100 BC, in the period of the judges. Unlike the violent and nationally striking tone of Judges, Ruth highlights ordinary life in Israel: families linked by clans and tribes, agricultural economy of livelihood and dependence on climate, with hunger as a real threat when the rains failed. The main scenario alternates between Moab, where Elimelch's family moves because of hunger, and Bethlehem, where Naomi returns when the crisis passes. The book reflects a simple, rural and socially vulnerable historical context.

structure.label: Hunger, migration and losses in Moabe
structure.description: The family of Elimelech leaves Bethlehem because of the famine; the death of her husband and children leaves Naomi in great help.

structure.label: Return to Bethlehem and Ruth's Loyalty
structure.description: Naomi decides to return home to the knowledge that the famine ceased; Ruth undertakes to accompany her and both arrive in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.

structure.label: Providence in the field of Boaz
structure.description: Ruth will respigate to support the house and finds Boaz's field, which responds generously when he discovers who she is.

structure.label: Rescue, marriage and descent
structure.description: Naomi advises Ruth to seek Boaz; he deals with the matter publicly at the door of the city, assumes redemption, marries Ruth and Obed is born, connected to David's lineage.

themes: Risk, courage and generosity in the life of faith
Redemption and protection through concrete responsibilities
Small acts with lasting impact on God's purpose
readingKeys: Notice how the book counters loss and restoration without resorting to major spectacular events: God's action appears in everyday gestures, prudent decisions and care relationships.
Pay attention to the speeches of blessing and commitment; they are not only godly words, but guide and interpret what happens in the plot.
Note the social sequence of the rescue: the field, the eira and the door of the city show that redemption is treated in a public, responsible and legal way, not just emotional.
profile.cautions: The authorship is not known for sure, and the historicity of the book was questioned by some scholars; yet, the introduction presented understands Ruth as firmly rooted in the historical and cultural context of Israel. For the evangelical reader, it is important to avoid readings that transform the book only into romance or moralism: its main emphasis is on God's providence operating in daily life. It is also appropriate to read the final genealogy as an integral part of the message, and not as an unimportant appendix.

dossier.narratedEra: The events are situated in the period of the judges, Around 1100 BC; Tyndale places the narrative between the death of Joshua and the beginning of Saul's reign in one Israel with few political structures and strong tribal and lynch life.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes indicate that the book was written after the events narrated, because certain customs were already forgotten at the time when the text was composed (Rt 4:7). The traditional authorship is probably attributed to Samuel by Matthew Henry, but Tyndale states that it is not known who wrote Ruth. The attached sources do not allow you to set an exact date of composition.

politics.title: Period of judges and absence of central political structures
politics.detail: The setting occurs when "Israel had few political structures" and the common life revolved more around tribal and clan ties than national identity. This helps to read Ruth as a domestic story situated in a world without a strong state controlling everyday life.
politics.readingImpact: The crisis of the Naoi family and the decisions of migration, work and marriage need to be read in a local and decentralized environment, not as a national policy.

politics.title: Transition between the time of the judges and the beginning of the monarchy
politics.detail: Tyndale defines the temporal frame as the period from Joshua's death to the beginning of Saul's reign, situating the events of Ruth around 1100 BC. Matthew Henry notes that the book comes before Samuel because he ends by introducing David.
politics.readingImpact: The book works as a historical bridge: it is born in the period of the judges, but already points to the lineage that flows into David.

politics.title: Public negotiation at the city door
politics.detail: Legal business, including property transfers, were made at the city's doorstep. Boaz uses this public space to solve the case of the nearest rescuer and formalize the transaction.
politics.readingImpact: The scene of chapter 4 is not just romance; it is a socially recognized legal act with witnesses and community legitimacy.

politics.title: Disputes for the right to redeem and protection of family property
politics.detail: The law of the ransomer preserved the land within the family; the closest relative had priority. Rute's presence alters the negotiation, because the rescue also involves the obligation to generate an heir for the name of the deceased and for the maintenance of the inheritance.
politics.readingImpact: The tension of chapter 4 depends on real family and property rights; the "no" of the relative illuminates the economic and social cost of preserving the Elimelech lineage.

customs.title: Hunger, migration and dependence on agriculture
customs.detail: The notes link hunger in Bethlehem to drought and explain that families depended on their own grains and animals for food and other needs. Moab could receive rain when the region of Judah did not receive.
customs.readingImpact: Elimeleque's trip to Moab is not arbitrary escape, but responds to real agricultural vulnerability.

customs.title: Respigar as a provision for the poor
customs.detail: The Law allowed us to leave what was left of the harvest for the poor to respigar. Ruth enters the field of Boaz within this custom, and Boaz goes beyond the legal minimum by favoring his harvest.
customs.readingImpact: Rute's work appears as dignity and survival, and Boaz's generosity gains weight of practical fidelity to the Torah.

customs.title: Harvest routine, shelters in the field and meal of workers
customs.detail: The workers used shelters along the fields for shadow and rest during the long journey. Boaz shares his meal with Ruth, and then directs the reapers to leave more for her.
customs.readingImpact: The book shows the common rural life with concrete details; divine grace is narrated in the midst of ordinary agricultural work.

customs.title: Sociability of home, clan and protection to vulnerable
customs.detail: Ruth puts himself down on the social scale when talking about "tuas servas," and Boaz assures that no one treats it with roughness or the expulsion of his field. The link between mother-in-law, nora and rescuer is read within the framework of the extended family.
customs.readingImpact: The relationship between the characters is not only personal; it depends on domestic hierarchies and the protection that an owner could offer.

customs.title: Rescuer and marriage linked to inheritance
customs.detail: The notes describe the gooel as a close male relative who helped a family member in economic difficulty. In Ruth, this connects to a close obligation of marriage by levirate in order to raise offspring for the deceased and to keep the land in the family.
customs.readingImpact: Boaz and Ruth's marriage is read as an act of family and economic allegiance, not just as an affective union.

language.title: Includes 1:6 and 4:13
language.detail: Tyndale notes that the same verb for "dar/allow" appears at the beginning and end of the story, framing the book with signs of providential action. This works as "bookends" literary.
language.readingImpact: The narrative asks to read the divine providence behind food, children and restoration, rather than just domestic coincidences.

language.title: "Rute, the moabita" as a repeated mark of alterity
language.detail: The author/author calls her "Rute," the Moabite five times. The repetition highlights that she was not Israeli and keeps her foreign condition alive.
language.readingImpact: Ruth's inclusion in the community and in David's lineage gains strength precisely because his foreign origin is never erased.

language.title: The verb "Apegate" in 1:14
language.detail: The verb used for Ruth to take care of Naomi is the same employee for the union of the man to the wife and for fidelity to the Lord in other biblical texts cited in the notes.
language.readingImpact: Ruth's loyalty is presented in language of alliance, not as mere family sympathy.

language.title: All-Powerful as translation of shadday
language.detail: The note explains that "Almighty" translates shadday, image linked to divine force and provision. Naomi protests in a real way, but history shows God's provision in a concrete way.
language.readingImpact: Noemi's lament is not corrected by negation, but put into tension with the divine ability to sustain and restore.

language.title: "On the days of then" and cultural memory
language.detail: In 4:7, the observation "in those days" is read as a sign that the custom of sandal was no longer known when the book was written. The literary detail helps date the text as later than the narrated events, without fixing the exact date.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the work talks to a community later, explaining old customs that already needed clarification.

timeline.title: The time of the judges, about 1100 BC.
timeline.detail: Tyndale places the events around 1100 BC, in the period of the judges, between the death of Joshua and the beginning of Saul's reign, around 1050 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The story reads as part of Israel's life before the monarchy, with social instability and local dependence.

timeline.title: Hunger in Bethlehem and outbound from Elimelech to Moab
timeline.detail: The narrative begins hungry in Bethlehem, explained in the notes as usually caused by drought in the Israeli plateau. The family migrates to Moab, where there was more chance of rain.
timeline.readingImpact: The departure of the family is motivated by concrete material crisis, which shapes the whole sequence of losses and returns.

timeline.title: Death of Elimelech and the two sons in Moab
timeline.detail: The sequence of deaths leaves Noemi without economic support and without heirs, which aggravates his social and family vulnerability.
timeline.readingImpact: The emotional climax of the introduction prepares the theme of restoration as a reversal of real loss, not abstract.

timeline.title: Return at the beginning of barley harvest
timeline.detail: The notes place the arrival of Noemi and Ruth in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest, between the end of March and mid-April by the current calendar.
timeline.readingImpact: The time of the return is providentially significant: the immediate need finds the moment of agricultural provision.

timeline.title: Writing later to the facts, with usual forgotten
timeline.detail: The 4:7 comment states that the book was not written immediately after the events, because the custom of the exchange of sandal had already fallen into oblivion. Matthew Henry also considers it likely that Samuel was the writer.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading must distinguish between the old setting and the posterior composition, without confusing the time of the plot with the time of the text.

timeline.title: Final Genealogy Coming to David
timeline.detail: The book ends with ten generations from Perez to David, and the notes highlight that Ruth's history serves the family history of the greatest king of Israel.
timeline.readingImpact: Genealogy gives historical horizon to the domestic narrative, connecting the restoration of a widow to the future of David.

investigation: Matthew Henry probably attributes authorship to Samuel, while Tyndale states that authorship is unknown; the dossier distinguishes tradition and textual uncertainty without inventing an exact date of composition.
Tyndale records that some scholars question Rute's historicity and suggest fiction, but the introduction itself argues that the work is firmly rooted in Israel's history and ancient life.
Ruth's notes are selective and pastoral: they clarify customs, language and providence, but do not bring an exhaustive historical reconstruction of the judges' period.
Several readings are inferential, especially when they link legal customs to the narrative function; they were marked as interpretation when the bond is not directly affirmed by the source.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the attached sources and therefore mainly reflects Tyndale's notes and the introduction of Matthew Henry. There is no basis here to accurately date the composition of the book beyond stating that it is later than the narrated events; Samuel's traditional authorship appears as probable, not certain. No independent archaeological chronologies or external historical reconstructions were incorporated. Some items depend on contextual inference from devotional and study notes, not independent historical demonstration. The controversies mentioned in the sources - especially about historicity and authorship - were preserved without an attempt to resolve the debate beyond what the notes support.
